docs.title: Practicals for the 2026 Genome Bioinformatics module
Introduction
docs.text:
Cheap sequencing has created the opportunity to perform molecular-genetic analyses on just about anything. Conceptually, doing this would be similar to working with traditional genetic model organisms. But a large difference exists: For traditional genetic model organisms, large teams and communities of expert assemblers, predictors, and curators have put years of efforts into the prerequisites for most genomic analyses, including a reference genome and a set of gene predictions. In contrast, those of us working on "emerging" model organisms often have limited or no pre-existing resources and are part of much smaller teams. Emerging model organisms includes most crops, animals and plant pest species, many pathogens, and major models for ecology & evolution.

At the end of this module, you should be able to:

  1. inspect and clean short (Illumina) reads,
  2. perform genome assembly,
  3. assess the quality of the genome assembly using simple statistics,
  4. predict protein-coding genes,
  5. assess quality of gene predictions,
  6. assess quality of the entire process using a biologically meaningful measure.

Info

Note: The exemplar datasets are simplified to run on laptops and to fit into the short format of this course. For real projects, much more sophisticated approaches are needed!

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Prerequisites for the practicals are:

  • a basic knowledge of Linux command line. For a refresher, try the SIB's UNIX fundamentals online course (here). You can also go through a Command Line Bootcamp.

  • a basic knowledge of R programming. The swirl() library course (here) can help. In particular, it can be useful:

    • following the R programming self-led course (skip the sections Simulation and Dates and Times)
    • following at least the ggplot section of the Exploratory_Data_Analysis swirl course.

docs.title: 2. Practicals
docs.text:
1. Short read cleaning: Illumina short read cleaning
  2. Reads to genome: genome assembly, quality control
  3. Gene prediction: gene prediction, quality control
  4. Population sequencing to genotypes to population genetics statistics:
    1. Mapping reads, calling variants, visualizing variant calls.
    2. Analysing variants: PCA, measuring differentiation & diversity.

What is an SSH-Key Pair?
docs.text:
To connect to Apocrita you will again be using SSH just like how you connected to your Virtual Machines (VMs). However, as Apocrita has a higher level of security you will need to use an SSH-Key Pair.

An SSH-Key Pair consists of two cryptographic keys: a public key and a private key.

These keys are used to securely authenticate your identity when connecting to remote servers, such as Apocrita.

  • The public key can be shared freely and is placed on the server you want to access.

  • The private key is kept secure on your own computer and should never be shared.

When you attempt to connect to a server using SSH, the server checks if your public key matches your private key. If they match, you are granted access. This method is more secure than using passwords alone.

docs.title: The Debugging Process
docs.text: When working with command-line tools it's common to run into issues / bugs. This guide provides a systematic approach to debugging common errors.

docs.title: Step 1. Switch on Your Virtual Machine
docs.text:
If you recieve the following error message: 

ssh: connect to host matt.genomicscourse.com port 22: Operation timed out

This indicates your AWS Virtual Machine (VM) is not yet switched on.

SOLUTION: To access your AWS Virtual Machine (VM) you have to first have to switch it on via the website switch.genomicscourse.com and wait 2-5 minutes for your machine to boot up!

docs.title: Step 2. Check you are connected to your VM
docs.text:
When you are connected to your AWS Virtual Machine (VM) there may be times when your connection drops and you are logged out. This can be due to:

  • Bad internet connection.
  • User inactivity.

How can you tell if you have become disconnected? You may see the following statement printed to your terminal:

Connection to matt.genomicscourse.com closed.
client_loop: send disconnect: Broken pipe

Also, it is important to check at the command-prompt (bottom of the terminal, where you type in your commands) your username should be the same as that provided by Vitaly and the host (after the @ symbol) should by an IP address.

matt@ip-172-31-38-337:~$

SOLUTION: If this happens, make sure to reconnect, via ssh to your AWS VM before continuing with the practical!

docs.title: Step 3. File Not Found
docs.text:
Let's say you are trying to run the command below:

fastqc --nogroup --outdir . input/reads.pe1.fastq.gz

However, you get an error message saying the file cannot be found, doesn't exist, or couldn't be read:

Skipping 'input/reads.pe1.fastq.gz' which didn't exist, or couldn't be read

When a command fails like this, follow these systematic steps to debug the problem:

  • Check your current directory: Use pwd (print working directory) to confirm where you are in the file system. Ensure you're in the correct location to run the command.

  • Verify the file exists: Use ls -l input/reads.pe1.fastq.gz to check if the file exists at the specified path. If you get a No such file or directory error, the file path is incorrect. Use the tree command to locate where your files actually are.

  • Check the file has content: Use ls -l to check the file size. If the size is 0, the file is empty, indicating a problem with a previous step. You can also use zcat input/reads.pe1.fastq.gz | head to preview the file contents.

SOLUTION: Once you've identified the issue using the steps above, you can:

  • Navigate to the correct directory using cd
  • Correct the file path in your command
  • Check if previous steps in your workflow completed successfully

docs.title: Step 4. Ask Colleagues / Your Neighbour
docs.text:
If you've tried the above steps and are still stuck, don't hesitate to ask for help from those around you:

  • Explain the problem: Describe what you're trying to do, what command you ran, and what error message you received. Often, articulating the problem helps you understand it better.

  • Share your screen or terminal output: Show your colleague the exact error message and the commands you've run. They may spot something you missed.

  • Compare approaches: Your neighbour might be using a slightly different approach that works, or they may have already solved a similar problem.

Remember: Collaboration is a key part of bioinformatics work. Helping each other debug problems is a valuable learning experience for everyone involved!

docs.title: Step 5. Ask an LLM (Large Language Model)
docs.text:
Modern AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, or GitHub Copilot can be helpful for debugging, but use them wisely:

  • Provide context: Share the error message, the command you ran, and relevant details about your environment.

  • Don't blindly follow suggestions: LLMs can make mistakes or provide solutions that don't apply to your specific situation. Always try to understand why the solution works.

  • Verify the solution: Test suggested fixes carefully and check that you understand each part of the command or code change.

  • Learn from the explanation: Ask the LLM to explain why the error occurred and how the solution addresses it. This helps build your debugging skills.

CAUTION: While LLMs are powerful tools, they should complement—not replace—your understanding. Always critically evaluate AI-generated solutions and ensure they make sense for your specific problem.

docs.title: Part 6 (Bonus) - Population Genomics on the Command Line
1. Introduction
docs.text:
In Part 5 you analysed the fire ant SNP data in R, using adegenet to draw a genotype heat map and PopGenome to calculate FST in sliding windows. You were given every line of code.

This bonus practical asks you to reach the same biological conclusions without R, and without being given the commands. You will use PLINK 2 - the standard command-line toolkit for population-scale genotype data - and then go beyond Part 5 by measuring linkage disequilibrium, the signature that most directly reveals a non-recombining supergene.

Your dataset is unchanged:

Genotype label Phenotype description Number of samples B single-queen colony 7 b multiple-queen colony 7

Fourteen haploid males, across two scaffolds taken from two different chromosomes.

Warning

This is a deliberately hard, self-directed exercise. Each section states a goal, not a recipe. Work out the commands yourself from plink2 --help, plink2 --help <flag-name> and the PLINK 2 documentation. Every section then offers a collapsed Hints box (flag names only) and, below it, a collapsed worked command. Open them in that order, and only after you have genuinely tried.

Info

No plots, no R. Every result in this practical is read directly in the terminal with head, awk, sort and column. Fourteen samples is small enough that the raw numbers are the visualisation - which is precisely why we can drop the graphics.

docs.title: 1.1. Fourteen samples is not many
docs.text:
Almost every design decision below follows from the sample size, so keep these in mind throughout:

  • Within a group of 7 haploids, an allele frequency can only take the values 0, 1/7, 2/7 ... 1. Across all 14, the step is 1/14. Your resolution is blunt.
  • A 10 kb window may contain only a couple of SNPs. A window average built from 2 SNPs is noise, not signal - you will have to filter these out yourself.
  • Linkage disequilibrium estimated from 14 haplotypes is coarse and biased upwards. Rare variants make this far worse, so they must be removed first.
  • With 7 versus 7 haploid genomes, however, a fixed difference (an allele present in all 7 B and absent from all 7 b) is unambiguous and easy to count. Small samples are bad at estimating frequencies but fine at detecting complete separation.

docs.title: 3. Challenge 1 - Get the Data Into PLINK 2
docs.text:
PLINK 2 does not work directly from a VCF for most analyses. It converts to its own binary format - a pfile, consisting of .pgen (genotypes), .pvar (variants) and .psam (samples) - and everything downstream reads that.

Task

Convert input/snp.vcf.gz into a pfile called tmp/snp.

Your first attempt will fail. That is intentional. Read PLINK's error message carefully and solve each problem in turn. You need to work out:

  • Why does PLINK reject our chromosome names? (Look at them: bcftools view -H input/snp.vcf.gz | cut -f1 | uniq)
  • Our VCF has . in the ID column. Several later analyses need unique variant IDs. How do you make PLINK generate them from chromosome and position?
  • How do you restrict the dataset to biallelic sites only?
Hints - Challenge 1

The four flags you need are among: --vcf, --allow-extra-chr, --set-all-var-ids, --max-alleles, --make-pgen, --out.

For --set-all-var-ids, the template characters @ and # stand for chromosome and position. Quote the template so the shell does not touch #.

Stuck? Worked command - Challenge 1 
plink2 \
  --vcf input/snp.vcf.gz \
  --allow-extra-chr \
  --set-all-var-ids '@:#' \
  --max-alleles 2 \
  --make-pgen \
  --out tmp/snp

Task

Verify the conversion rather than trusting it. Compare PLINK's reported counts against the VCF itself:

bcftools view -H input/snp.vcf.gz | wc -l   # variants in the VCF
bcftools query -l input/snp.vcf.gz | wc -l  # samples in the VCF
head -n 3 tmp/snp.pvar
cat tmp/snp.psam

Question

QuestionAnswer
  • How many samples and variants did PLINK load, and do they match the VCF?
  • If the variant count dropped, which flag caused it and is that acceptable?
  • Look at tmp/snp.psam. What are the sample IDs, and what happened to the family ID (FID) column?
  • You should have 14 samples. The variant count should match the VCF unless there were multiallelic sites.
  • Any drop is caused by --max-alleles 2. It is acceptable here: r² and most FST estimators are only defined for biallelic markers, and multiallelic sites in a 14-sample haploid dataset are almost always alignment artefacts.
  • The IDs are the original VCF sample names, still carrying the .bam suffix (e.g. f1_B.bam). There is no FID column at all - the header starts #IID - because a VCF has no family structure, so PLINK 2 does not invent one. You must use the full ID including .bam in every file you write from now on.

docs.title: 4. Challenge 2 - Describe the Dataset and Define the Two Groups
docs.text:
Before any population comparison, find out what you are working with: how much data is missing, and how variable the SNPs actually are.

Task

Using your pfile, produce (a) an allele-frequency report and (b) a per-sample missingness report. Then look at both.

Hints - Challenge 2a

--pfile to load the data, then --freq and --missing. Remember --allow-extra-chr is needed on every PLINK command with this dataset. The outputs are .afreq, .smiss and .vmiss files.

Stuck? Worked commands - Challenge 2a 
plink2 --pfile tmp/snp --allow-extra-chr --freq    --out tmp/snp
plink2 --pfile tmp/snp --allow-extra-chr --missing --out tmp/snp

head tmp/snp.afreq
column -t tmp/snp.smiss

Question

QuestionAnswer
  • Look at the ALT_FREQS column of tmp/snp.afreq. What is the smallest non-zero value you can see, and why can it not be any smaller?
  • Does any sample have unusually high missingness? What would you do about it if one did?
  • The smallest non-zero frequency is 1/14 ≈ 0.0714: one alternative allele among 14 haploid males. (Strictly, PLINK stores each haploid call as a homozygous diploid, so it counts 2 of 28 alleles - but the frequency is the same.) Frequencies move in fourteenths - there is no such thing as a 1% allele in this dataset.
  • With 14 samples, a single poorly sequenced individual removes 7% of the information and can distort every group comparison. If one stood out you would exclude it with --remove and re-run everything downstream.

docs.title: 4.1. Defining the populations
docs.text:
PLINK has no idea which sample is B and which is b. You must tell it, using a phenotype file: a tab-separated table whose header line begins with #IID, with one row per sample.

Task

Write tmp/populations.tsv with two columns - the sample ID and a POP column containing B or b.

Do not type it out by hand. Generate it from tmp/snp.psam so that it can never disagree with the actual sample list. The B samples are the ones whose ID ends in _B.bam.

Hints - Challenge 2b

awk with a conditional expression: cond ? "B" : "b". Skip the .psam header with NR>1. Prepend the header line with printf '#IID\tPOP\n' and group the two commands with { ... ; } > file.

Stuck? Worked command - Challenge 2b 
{ printf '#IID\tPOP\n'
  awk 'NR>1 { print $1"\t"( $1 ~ /_B\.bam$/ ? "B" : "b" ) }' tmp/snp.psam
} > tmp/populations.tsv

column -t tmp/populations.tsv

Task

You will also need two sample ID files so that later commands can be restricted to one group at a time. Create tmp/keep_B.txt and tmp/keep_b.txt, each containing a #IID header followed by the IDs of that group only.

Stuck? Worked command - Challenge 2c 
for pop in B b; do
  { printf '#IID\n'
    awk -v p="$pop" 'NR>1 && $2==p { print $1 }' tmp/populations.tsv
  } > tmp/keep_${pop}.txt
done

wc -l tmp/keep_B.txt tmp/keep_b.txt

Question

QuestionAnswer

Each keep file should have 8 lines. Why 8 and not 7?

Seven sample IDs plus the #IID header line. PLINK 2 uses that header to work out that the file contains IIDs only rather than FID/IID pairs - if you omit it, PLINK will try to interpret your single column as a family ID and match nothing.

docs.title: 5. Challenge 3 - Who Resembles Whom? A Genetic Relationship Matrix
docs.text:
In Part 5 you drew a genotype heat map and a PCA to ask a single question: do the B and b individuals fall into two genetic groups, and does that depend on which scaffold you look at?

With 14 samples there is a more direct answer that needs no graphics at all. Ask PLINK for the genetic relationship between every pair of samples. The result is a 14 × 14 matrix - small enough to read straight off the screen.

Each off-diagonal value compares two samples across all SNPs, after scaling each SNP by its allele frequency:

  • positive - the pair share more alleles than expected by chance;
  • around 0 - no more or less similar than two random samples;
  • negative - the pair share fewer alleles than expected.

The diagonal is each sample compared with itself, so it is close to 1.

Task

Compute a genetic relationship matrix (GRM) for all samples and write it as a full square matrix to results/rel_all.

If PLINK refuses to run, read the error carefully. With only 14 samples it does not trust frequencies it estimates on the fly - but you already made a frequency file in Challenge 2.

Hints - Challenge 3a

Look up --make-rel with plink2 --help make-rel. The square modifier controls the output shape.

--read-freq supplies a pre-computed .afreq file. --mac 1 drops sites with no minor allele, which carry no information about relatedness.

The command writes two files: the numbers (.rel), and the sample IDs in matrix order (.rel.id).

Note: if you search online you will find --distance. That is a PLINK 1.9 flag and does not exist in PLINK 2.

Stuck? Worked command - Challenge 3a 
plink2 \
  --pfile tmp/snp \
  --allow-extra-chr \
  --read-freq tmp/snp.afreq \
  --mac 1 \
  --make-rel square \
  --out results/rel_all

Task

The matrix file has no row labels and far too many decimal places. Glue the sample IDs onto the front of each row, round the values to 2 decimal places, and line up the columns.

Inspect results/rel_all.rel.id first: does it start with a # header line that you need to skip?

Notice that the samples alternate f1_B, f1b, f2_B, f2b ... Before you look at the numbers, predict what pattern two genetic groups would produce in a matrix whose rows and columns alternate between groups.

Stuck? Worked command - Challenge 3b 
paste <(awk '!/^#/ { print $NF }' results/rel_all.rel.id) \
      <(awk '{ for (i=1; i<=NF; i++) printf "%.2f%s", $i, (i<NF ? "\t" : "\n") }' results/rel_all.rel) \
  | column -t

Task

Now repeat the whole thing one scaffold at a time. This is the crucial comparison - it is the command-line equivalent of the two separate heat maps you made in Part 5.

Do not assume you know which scaffold carries the supergene. Let the numbers tell you.

Hints - Challenge 3c

--chr <name> restricts an analysis to one chromosome/scaffold. Wrap the two runs in a for loop over scaffold_1 scaffold_2.

Stuck? Worked command - Challenge 3c 
for sc in scaffold_1 scaffold_2; do
  plink2 \
    --pfile tmp/snp \
    --allow-extra-chr \
    --chr "$sc" \
    --read-freq tmp/snp.afreq \
    --mac 1 \
    --make-rel square \
    --out "results/rel_${sc}"

  echo "=== $sc ==="
  paste <(awk '!/^#/ { print $NF }' results/rel_${sc}.rel.id) \
        <(awk '{ for (i=1; i<=NF; i++) printf "%.2f%s", $i, (i<NF ? "\t" : "\n") }' results/rel_${sc}.rel) \
    | column -t
done

Question

QuestionAnswer
  • On which scaffold do B–B and b–b values differ consistently from B–b values? Describe the pattern.
  • On the other scaffold, do samples still form groups? If so, are those groups related to colony type?
  • On the supergene scaffold, compare the b–b values with the b diagonal values, then do the same for B. Which group is more genetically uniform? Which Part 5 result does this reproduce?
  • This matrix contains the same information as the Part 5 heat map and PCA. Why would this approach stop working if you had 500 samples instead of 14?
  • scaffold_1. It is a perfect checkerboard: every B–b value is about -1.2, every b–b value is about +1.25, and every B–B value is positive (roughly 0.7 to 2.2). The 14 samples fall into two genetic groups that exactly match the phenotype labels. (Sorting the rows so all B come first would turn the checkerboard into two solid blocks.)
  • Yes, but not by colony type. On scaffold_2, pairs such as f2_B/f2b and f7_B/f7b are almost identical to each other, and six samples of both types (f1b, f3_B, f3b, f4_B, f4b, f6b) form a tight cluster. This is the ordinary relatedness and haplotype sharing you expect on a freely recombining chromosome, and it cuts straight across the B/b labels.
  • On scaffold_1, the b–b values (~1.25) are nearly as high as the b diagonal (~1.27-1.33): every b is almost identical to every other b. The B diagonals (2.2-3.5) are much higher than the B–B values, so B individuals differ from each other. This is the low diversity of the b supergene haplotype that PopGenome measured in Part 5.
  • With 500 samples the matrix has 250,000 entries and cannot be read by eye. That is exactly the problem PCA solves: PLINK's --pca is an eigen-decomposition of this same relationship matrix, compressing it into a handful of coordinates that can be plotted. Our sample size is small enough that we can skip the compression step entirely.

docs.title: 6. Challenge 4 - Genetic Differentiation (FST)
docs.text:
FST measures how differentiated two groups are at a locus: 0 means the groups are identical, 1 means they share no alleles at all. In Part 5, PopGenome gave you FST averaged over sliding windows.

Warning

PLINK 2 has no sliding-window FST option. It will give you FST per variant; turning that into windows is your job. Do not waste time looking for a --fst-window-size flag - it does not exist.

docs.title: 6.1. Per-variant FST
docs.text:
Task

Calculate FST between B and b for every SNP. You need to:

  • load the population labels from tmp/populations.tsv;
  • tell PLINK which column of that file defines the groups;
  • request the Hudson estimator rather than the default;
  • ask for per-variant output as well as the summary.

Then find out what PLINK actually wrote - the filenames include the population names, so do not guess:

ls results/fst*
Hints - Challenge 4a

--pheno loads the file, --pheno-name picks the column, and --fst takes the name of that same column plus modifiers. Look up the modifiers with plink2 --help fst: you want method=hudson and report-variants.

A phenotype column containing non-numeric values such as B/b is loaded as a categorical phenotype, which is what --fst requires.

Stuck? Worked command - Challenge 4a 
plink2 \
  --pfile tmp/snp \
  --allow-extra-chr \
  --pheno tmp/populations.tsv \
  --pheno-name POP \
  --fst POP method=hudson report-variants \
  --out results/fst

ls results/fst*
head results/fst.*.fst.var
cat  results/fst.fst.summary

Question

QuestionAnswer

Why does the choice of estimator matter more here than it would in a study of 2,000 humans? (Hint: read what plink2 --help fst says about the two methods.)

The Weir–Cockerham and Hudson estimators differ mainly in how they correct for finite sample size. With 7 haplotypes per group those corrections are large relative to the quantity being estimated, so the two methods can give noticeably different numbers. The Hudson estimator is less sensitive to small and unequal sample sizes, which is why it is preferred here. With thousands of samples the correction is negligible and the choice barely matters.

docs.title: 6.2. Building your own windows
docs.text:
Task

Turn the per-variant file into 10 kb non-overlapping windows, reporting for each window: scaffold, start, end, number of SNPs, and mean FST.

Two traps to handle:

  • The FST column is not in the same position in every PLINK version. Find it from the header line rather than hard-coding a field number.
  • Monomorphic sites give nan. One nan will poison an entire window average.
  • Finally - and most importantly - discard windows built from only a handful of SNPs before you rank anything.
Hints - Challenge 4b

int($pos/10000) gives the window index. Build a key from scaffold plus window index, accumulate sum[key] and n[key], and print in an END block. Test a numeric value with ($x+0==$x), which is false for nan.

Stuck? Worked command - Challenge 4b 
awk -F'\t' '
  NR==1 { for (i=1; i<=NF; i++) { if ($i ~ /FST$/) f=i; if ($i=="POS") p=i }; next }
  ($f+0==$f) {
    w = int($p/10000)
    key = $1"\t"(w*10000)"\t"((w+1)*10000)
    sum[key] += $f; n[key]++
  }
  END { for (k in sum) if (n[k] >= 5) printf "%s\t%d\t%.4f\n", k, n[k], sum[k]/n[k] }
' results/fst.*.fst.var \
  | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n \
  > results/fst_windows.tsv

head results/fst_windows.tsv

Task

Now interrogate the table from the shell. Work out how to:

  • rank all windows by mean FST and show the top 10;
  • compute the mean FST separately for each scaffold.
Stuck? Worked commands - Challenge 4c 
# Top 10 windows genome-wide
sort -k5,5gr results/fst_windows.tsv | head -n 10 | column -t

# Mean FST and window count per scaffold
awk '{ s[$1]+=$5; c[$1]++ } END { for (k in s) printf "%s\tn_windows=%d\tmean_FST=%.4f\n", k, c[k], s[k]/c[k] }' \
  results/fst_windows.tsv

Question

QuestionAnswer
  • Which scaffold holds the high-FST windows?
  • Re-run the windowing step with the n[k] >= 5 filter removed. What happens to the top of the ranked list, and why?
  • B and b do not recombine with one another in one region of the genome. Explain the FST pattern in that light.
  • scaffold_1: every one of the top 10 windows is on it, and its mean window FST is about 0.67, compared with about 0.02 on scaffold_2. The genome-wide summary (about 0.63) is dominated by scaffold_1.
  • Without the filter, the top of the list fills with windows containing one or two SNPs and an FST of exactly 1. A single SNP that happens to be fixed between the groups gives a perfect window average, but it is one observation from 14 haplotypes - it tells you almost nothing. Minimum-SNP filters are not cosmetic; with small samples they are what separates signal from arithmetic.
  • scaffold_1 contains the supergene. Because recombination between the B and b haplotypes is suppressed, mutations arising on one haplotype can never be shuffled onto the other, so differences accumulate and become fixed - driving FST up across the whole region. scaffold_2 recombines normally, so alleles continue to be shared between the groups and FST stays near zero.

docs.title: 6.3. Counting fixed differences
docs.text:
FST is a summary statistic. With haploid data and clean groups you can ask something more concrete: at how many SNPs does every single B carry one allele and every single b the other?

Task

Calculate allele frequencies separately for each group, then compare them. Use the keep-files from Challenge 2.

Hints - Challenge 4d

--keep restricts a run to the listed samples. Loop over B and b, writing tmp/freq_B.afreq and tmp/freq_b.afreq. A fixed difference is a variant where ALT_FREQS is 1 in one group and 0 in the other.

Stuck? Worked commands - Challenge 4e 
for pop in B b; do
  plink2 \
    --pfile tmp/snp \
    --allow-extra-chr \
    --keep tmp/keep_${pop}.txt \
    --freq \
    --out tmp/freq_${pop}
done

awk '
  FNR==1 { for (i=1; i<=NF; i++) col[$i]=i; id=col["ID"]; fq=col["ALT_FREQS"]; ch=col["#CHROM"]; next }
  NR==FNR { fB[$id]=$fq; chrom[$id]=$ch; next }
  ($id in fB) {
    total[chrom[$id]]++
    if ((fB[$id]+0==1 && $fq+0==0) || (fB[$id]+0==0 && $fq+0==1)) fixed[chrom[$id]]++
  }
  END { for (c in total) printf "%s\tSNPs=%d\tfixed_differences=%d\t(%.1f%%)\n", c, total[c], fixed[c], 100*fixed[c]/total[c] }
' tmp/freq_B.afreq tmp/freq_b.afreq

Question

QuestionAnswer
  • How many fixed differences are there on each scaffold?
  • A sceptic says: "with only 7 samples per group, some of those apparent fixed differences are luck." Are they right, and does that objection apply equally to both scaffolds?
  • scaffold_1 has about 524 fixed differences - nearly half of its 1,106 SNPs. scaffold_2 has none.
  • The sceptic has a fair point in principle: a variant at 80% frequency in a large population can easily appear in all 7 sampled B individuals by chance. For any single SNP the evidence is weak. But the objection does not explain what you see: chance cannot produce hundreds of fixed differences concentrated in one contiguous region of one scaffold while the other scaffold has none. The clustering, not the individual SNPs, is what makes the result convincing - and it is why the next section, which looks at how those SNPs are linked together, matters so much.

docs.title: 7. Challenge 5 - Linkage Disequilibrium (Going Beyond Part 5)
docs.text:
Everything so far tells you that B and b differ on scaffold_1. It does not directly show why. The supergene hypothesis makes a specific, testable prediction about linkage disequilibrium (LD): the non-random association between alleles at different positions, measured as r².

Under normal recombination, LD decays with physical distance - nearby SNPs are correlated, distant ones are not. Inside a region where recombination is suppressed, the whole block is inherited as a single unit, so r² stays high no matter how far apart the SNPs are.

Warning

LD from 14 haplotypes is noisy and biased upwards, and rare alleles make this much worse: a variant seen in a single individual is perfectly correlated with every other singleton in that individual, by construction. You must apply a minor-allele-frequency filter before computing r², or your results are an artefact.

docs.title: 7.1. Calculating r²
docs.text:
Task

For each scaffold separately, calculate r² between pairs of SNPs, having first removed low-frequency variants.

You will need to work out:

  • which r² flag suits unphased genotype data;
  • how to stop PLINK discarding pairs below its default r² threshold (you want the low values too - they are the whole point of a decay curve);
  • how to stop PLINK limiting pairs by variant count and by distance, so that you get comparisons spanning the full scaffold;
  • what MAF threshold corresponds to "seen in at least 2 of the 14 samples".
Hints - Challenge 5a

--r2-unphased is the calculation. The relevant windowing flags are --ld-window, --ld-window-kb and --ld-window-r2; check their defaults with plink2 --help ld-window, because the defaults are designed for human genome-wide data and will silently throw away most of your pairs.

--maf sets the frequency filter. 2/14 ≈ 0.14.

Run ls results/ld_* afterwards - work out the output extension rather than assuming it.

Stuck? Worked command - Challenge 5a 
for sc in scaffold_1 scaffold_2; do
  plink2 \
    --pfile tmp/snp \
    --allow-extra-chr \
    --chr "$sc" \
    --maf 0.14 \
    --r2-unphased \
    --ld-window 100000 \
    --ld-window-kb 10000 \
    --ld-window-r2 0 \
    --out "results/ld_${sc}"
done

ls results/ld_*
head results/ld_scaffold_1.vcor

Question

QuestionAnswer

Before you look at any r² values, predict: in Challenge 4 you found that around half the SNPs on scaffold_1 are fixed differences between B and b. What must r² be between any two of those SNPs, and how should that depend on the distance between them?

Exactly 1, at any distance. Every fixed-difference SNP splits the 14 samples into the same two groups (the 7 B and the 7 b), so knowing the allele at one tells you the allele at every other with certainty. With around 500 such SNPs, roughly a third of all scaffold_1 pairs should have r² = 1 regardless of distance. Look for this in the next step.

docs.title: 7.2. LD decay with distance
docs.text:
Task

Build an LD decay table: group SNP pairs by the physical distance between them (for example in 10 kb bins), and report for each bin the number of pairs, the mean r², and the proportion of pairs in near-perfect LD (r² ≥ 0.8).

As in Challenge 4, locate the columns from the header line rather than hard-coding positions, and require a minimum number of pairs per bin.

Hints - Challenge 5b

The columns you need are the two positions and the r² value; the r² header ends in R2. Distance is the absolute difference between the positions. The bin index is int(distance/10000). Keep a third counter for pairs with r² ≥ 0.8.

Stuck? Worked command - Challenge 5b 
for sc in scaffold_1 scaffold_2; do
  echo "=== $sc ==="
  awk -F'\t' '
    NR==1 { for (i=1;i<=NF;i++) { if ($i ~ /R2$/) r=i; if ($i=="POS_A") a=i; if ($i=="POS_B") b=i }; next }
    ($r+0==$r) {
      d = ($b > $a) ? $b-$a : $a-$b
      k = int(d/10000)
      sum[k] += $r; n[k]++; if ($r >= 0.8) hi[k]++
      if (k > maxk) maxk = k
    }
    END {
      printf "%-14s %8s %10s %12s\n", "distance_kb", "n_pairs", "mean_r2", "prop_r2>=0.8"
      for (k=0; k<=maxk; k++) if (n[k] >= 20)
        printf "%-14s %8d %10.3f %12.3f\n", (k*10)"-"((k+1)*10), n[k], sum[k]/n[k], hi[k]/n[k]
    }
  ' results/ld_${sc}.vcor
done

Question

QuestionAnswer
  • Does mean r² decay with distance on either scaffold across the ~200 kb you have?
  • Which scaffold has consistently higher r², and higher proportion of near-perfect pairs? Does that change with distance?
  • scaffold_2 recombines normally, yet its r² (~0.3) is far above what unlinked SNPs should show. Look back at its relationship matrix in Challenge 3. What might be inflating LD?
  • Why is LD a more direct test of the supergene hypothesis than FST?
  • Not in any clear way. scaffold_1 sits at about 0.55 and scaffold_2 at about 0.30 across every bin; scaffold_2 drops only slightly from its first bin (about 0.36 at 0-10 kb). A 200 kb scaffold and 14 samples are simply not enough to trace a full decay curve - an honest and important limitation.
  • scaffold_1, at every distance. Roughly a third of its pairs (0.30-0.41) have r² ≥ 0.8 whether they are 5 kb or 195 kb apart, against 0.06-0.15 on scaffold_2. This is your prediction from 7.1 coming true: the fixed-difference SNPs are all in perfect LD with each other, 10 bp or 190 kb apart. Nothing has broken the B and b haplotypes up.
  • Relatedness. The relationship matrix showed near-identical pairs (f2_B/f2b, f7_B/f7b) and a tight six-sample cluster. Related individuals share long stretches of chromosome, which creates LD between distant SNPs even where recombination is normal. With 14 samples, a few such pairs are enough to lift the whole curve. This is also why PLINK warns about estimating LD from fewer than 50 samples.
  • High FST says the groups differ, but drift, isolation or selection can all produce that. The LD result is more specific: across the whole of scaffold_1, the same two haplotypes persist intact over the full length of the scaffold. That is what suppressed recombination - the defining property of a supergene - looks like.

docs.title: 7.3. Pruning: does the signal survive?
docs.text:
A fair criticism of Challenge 3 is that your relationship matrix counted hundreds of scaffold_1 SNPs that are all telling you the same thing, because they are in perfect LD. Effectively, you may have counted one piece of evidence many times.

Task

Use LD-based pruning to retain an approximately independent subset of SNPs, then rebuild the scaffold_1 relationship matrix using only those SNPs. Does the B/b checkerboard survive?

PLINK will refuse to prune this dataset. Read the error message in full. It tells you how to override it - but before you do, decide whether overriding is justified here, and write your reasoning in WHATIDID.txt.

Hints - Challenge 5c

--indep-pairwise takes a window size, a step size and an r² threshold, and writes .prune.in (keep) and .prune.out (drop). Feed the .prune.in list back into a later run with --extract. The override flag is named in the error message.

Stuck? Worked commands - Challenge 5c 
# --bad-ld: fewer than 50 samples; acceptable for an exploratory check only
plink2 \
  --pfile tmp/snp \
  --allow-extra-chr \
  --bad-ld \
  --indep-pairwise 50kb 1 0.5 \
  --out tmp/pruned

# Kept / removed per scaffold (IDs are CHROM:POS)
cut -d: -f1 tmp/pruned.prune.in  | sort | uniq -c
cut -d: -f1 tmp/pruned.prune.out | sort | uniq -c

plink2 \
  --pfile tmp/snp \
  --allow-extra-chr \
  --chr scaffold_1 \
  --extract tmp/pruned.prune.in \
  --read-freq tmp/snp.afreq \
  --mac 1 \
  --make-rel square \
  --out results/rel_scaffold_1_pruned

paste <(awk '!/^#/ { print $NF }' results/rel_scaffold_1_pruned.rel.id) \
      <(awk '{ for (i=1; i<=NF; i++) printf "%.2f%s", $i, (i<NF ? "\t" : "\n") }' results/rel_scaffold_1_pruned.rel) \
  | column -t

Question

QuestionAnswer
  • Why does PLINK refuse to prune fewer than 50 samples, and was it reasonable to override it here?
  • What proportion of each scaffold's SNPs survives pruning? Is that what you expected for a supergene versus an ordinary chromosome?
  • Is the B/b split still visible in the pruned relationship matrix? What has changed?
  • A colleague suggests always pruning before calculating FST. Would you agree, for this dataset?
  • Pruning decisions depend entirely on r², and r² from 14 samples is noisy and inflated, so PLINK over-prunes. Here it removed 1,794 of 1,859 SNPs (about 96%). Overriding is defensible for an exploratory check whose conclusion does not hinge on exactly which SNPs survive, but you should not use these pruned sets in a published analysis without saying so.
  • About 4% survive on both scaffolds (42 of 1,106 on scaffold_1, 23 of 753 on scaffold_2). You might have expected the supergene to lose far more, but the relatedness that inflated r² on scaffold_2 in 7.2 pushes almost every pair there above 0.5 as well. At this sample size pruning cannot tell the two scaffolds apart - a direct demonstration of why PLINK issued the warning.
  • Partly. The b samples still form a tight group (every b–b value is positive) and every B–b value is still negative. But the B–B values are now scattered around 0: B individuals no longer look alike. Pruning collapsed the ~500 fixed differences - the SNPs that made every B resemble every other B - down to a handful, so what remains is mostly variation within B. The split is weaker because the "redundant" SNPs were the signal.
  • No. Pruning is designed for analyses that assume independent markers, such as PCA or association testing. Here, the clustering of differentiated SNPs is the finding - as the pruned matrix just showed, pruning them away discards the evidence you are trying to measure. Choose to prune based on what the analysis assumes, not out of habit.

docs.title: 8. Wrap-Up
docs.text:
Question

QuestionAnswer

Using only the numbers you generated in this practical - no plots - write three sentences summarising what you have learned about the two scaffolds.

scaffold_2 behaves like an ordinary chromosome: relationships between samples reflect relatedness rather than colony type, FST between B and b is near zero, and there are no fixed differences. scaffold_1 behaves like a supergene: samples split cleanly into B and b, the b haplotype is almost invariant, FST is high across the whole scaffold, around half its SNPs are fixed between the groups, and r² stays high over the full length of the scaffold. That persistent LD is the key observation, because it points to suppressed recombination as the cause of the differentiation rather than merely another symptom of it.

Task

Check that WHATIDID.txt contains every command you actually ran, including the ones that failed and what you changed. A colleague should be able to reproduce all of your results from that file alone.

docs.title: Files you should have produced
docs.text:
Terminal

results/
├── rel_all.rel / .rel.id                    # 14x14 relationship matrix, all SNPs
├── rel_scaffold_1.rel / .rel.id             # ... scaffold_1 only
├── rel_scaffold_2.rel / .rel.id             # ... scaffold_2 only
├── rel_scaffold_1_pruned.rel / .rel.id      # ... after LD pruning
├── fst.fst.summary                          # genome-wide FST summary
├── fst.B.b.fst.var                          # per-variant FST
├── fst_windows.tsv                          # your 10 kb windowed FST table
├── ld_scaffold_1.vcor                       # pairwise r2, scaffold_1
└── ld_scaffold_2.vcor                       # pairwise r2, scaffold_2

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Throughout this tutorial, you'll uncover 22 hidden characters—each one a piece of a secret word. Tackle each challenge below to reveal the next character. Ready to sharpen your skills and solve the puzzle? Let the hunt begin!

docs.title: Preparations
docs.text:
Task

Create a new directory UNIX_Skills_Recap and then copy the exercises directory /shared/data/bash_tutorial/exercises into UNIX_Skills_Recap

mkdir UNIX_Skills_Recap
cd ./UNIX_Skills_Recap
cp -r /shared/data/bash_tutorial/exercises .

The steps outlined below shall be completed in the ./UNIX_Skills_Recap directory.

docs.title: 1.1. Navigating directories
docs.text:
The first character is hidden in a file somewhere in the exercise1 directory tree. Use the commands

cd <directory_name>

(do not type the pointy brackets, just insert the directory name) and

ls

to move from one directory to the next. Look through subdirectories until you find one with the name solution_1.1 and list its contents. If you went to a wrong directory, you can go back one level by typing:

cd ..

or go back to your home folder:

cd

docs.title: 1.2. Show a hidden file
docs.text:
Some files are not visible immediately. To see them, you need the command

ls -a

The second character, is in the same directory as the first one, but in a hidden file.

docs.title: 1.3. Execute a program
docs.text:
Use cd .. to go back to the directory exercise_1/directoryB/. When listing its contents, you should see a shell script file program.sh. To find the third character, you need to execute the program. On bash, this is done by typing source and the name of the program:

source program.sh

docs.title: 1.4. Find out how big a file is
docs.text:
Go to the folder exercise_1/directoryC/. To find the fourth character, you need to find out how big the text file in the directory is. This is done with the command

ls -l

docs.title: Part 1: Introduction To Genomic Data & Read Cleaning
1. Introduction
docs.text:
Cheap sequencing has created the opportunity to perform molecular-genetic analyses on almost anything! Traditional model organisms including C. elegans, S. cerevisiae (Yeast) & D. melanogaster (Fruit Fly) to name a few, benefited from years of efforts by expert genome assemblers, gene predictors, and curators. They have created most of the prerequisites for genomic analyses.

In contrast, genomic resources are much more limited for those working on "emerging" model organisms or other species. These new organisms include most crops, animals and plant pest species, many pathogens, and major models for ecology & evolution.

The steps below are meant to provide some ideas that can help obtaining a reference genome and geneset of sufficient quality for many analyses. They are based on worked performed by the Wurm Lab who assembled the fire ant genome [1].

In this pratical, the dataset you will use represents ~0.5% of the fire ant genome. This enables us to perform a toy/sandbox version of all analyses within a much shorter time than would normally be required.

During this series of practicals, we will:

  1. Inspect and clean short (Illumina) reads,
  2. Perform genome assemble using our 'cleaned' data.
  3. Assess the quality of our genome assembly.
  4. Identify protein-coding genes within our assembly.
  5. Assess the quality of gene predictions.
  6. Assess the quality of the entire process using a biologically meaningful measure.

Note: Please do not jump ahead. You will gain the most by following through each section of the practical one by one. If you're fast, dig deeper into particular aspects. Dozens of approaches and tools exist for each step - try to understand their tradeoffs.

Now we will start by creating a directory (folder) to work in!

Drawing on ideas from Noble (2009)[2] and others, we recommend following a specific directory convention for all your projects. The details of the convention that we will use in this practical can be found here. For the purpose of this practical we will use a slightly simplified version of this structure which is now explained below.

  • Inside this directory, create other three directories, called input, tmp, and results.

  • The directory results will contain a copy of the final results.

Now, see if you can make the necessary input, tmp and results subdirectories on your own!

Info

Being disciplined about structuring analyses is extremely important. It is similar to having a laboratory notebook. It will prevent you from becoming overwhelmed by having too many files, or not remembering what you did where.

docs.title: 4. Sequencing an appropriate sample
docs.text:
The properties of your data can affect the ability of bioinformatics algorithms to handle them. For instance, less diversity and complexity in a sample makes life easier: assembly algorithms really struggle when given similar sequences. So less heterozygosity and fewer repeats are easier.

Thus:

  • A haploid is easier than a diploid (those of us working on haplo-diploid Hymenoptera have it easy because male ants are haploid).
  • It goes without saying that a diploid is easier than a tetraploid!
  • An inbred line or strain is easier than a wild-type.
  • A more compact genome (with less repetitive DNA) is easier than one full of repeats - sorry, grasshopper & tick researchers! ;)

Many considerations go into the appropriate experimental design and sequencing strategy. We will not formally cover those here as this is a simple introduction and instead jump right into getting hands on with our data!

docs.title: 5. Illumina short-read cleaning
docs.text:
In this practical, we will work with paired ends short read sequences from an Illumina machine. Each piece of DNA was thus sequenced once from the 5' and once from the 3' end. Thus, we expect to have two files per sequence.

However, sequencers aren't perfect. Several problems may affect the quality of the reads. You can find some examples here and here.

Also, as you may already know, "garbage in – garbage out", which means that reads should be cleaned before performing any analysis.

docs.title: Setup and initial inspection using FastQC
docs.text:
Lets move to the main directory for this practical, so that everything we need and do and create is in one place:

Task

# Remember that yours may have a different date, now or in future, so be careful to check if you copy-paste code
cd ~/2026-09-22-read_cleaning

After, create a symbolic link (or symlink) using ln -s from the reads files to the input directory us the commands below:

# Change directory to input
cd input

# Link the two compressed FASTQ files (remember that each correspond to one of
# the pair)
ln -s /shared/data/reads.pe1.fastq.gz .
ln -s /shared/data/reads.pe2.fastq.gz .

# Return to the main directory
cd ..

Now run the tree command to inspect your directory structure.

The structure of your directory should look like this:

Terminal

2026-09-22-read_cleaning
├── input
│   ├── reads.pe1.fastq.gz -> /shared/data/reads.pe1.fastq.gz
│   └── reads.pe2.fastq.gz -> /shared/data/reads.pe2.fastq.gz
├── tmp
├── results
└── WHATIDID.txt

Now, you can start evaluating the quality of the reads reads.pe1.fastq.gz and reads.pe2.fastq.gz. To do so, we will use FastQC (documentation). FastQC is a bioinformatics software tool to help visualise the characteristics of a sequencing run. It can thus inform your read cleaning a.k.a your quality control strategy.

Task

Run FastQC on the reads.pe1.fastq.gz and reads.pe2.fastq.gz files. The command is given below, where instead of YOUR_OUTDIR, you will need replace YOUR_OUTDIR with the path to your tmp directory (e.g. if you main directory is 2026-09-22-read_cleaning, you need to replace YOUR_OUTDIR with tmp):

fastqc --nogroup --outdir YOUR_OUTDIR input/reads.pe1.fastq.gz

The --nogroup option ensures that bases are not grouped together in many of the plots generated by FastQC. This makes it easier to interpret the output in many cases. The --outdir option is there to help you clearly separate input and output files. To learn more about these options run fastqc --help in the terminal.

Important Note - Remember to log the commands you used in the WHATIDID.txt file. To do this you can use the text editors introduced in the UNIX practical including nano

Take a moment to verify your directory structure. You can do so using the tree command (be aware of your current working directory using the command pwd):

tree ~/2026-09-22-read_cleaning

The resulting directory structure should look like this:

Terminal

├── input
│   ├── reads.pe1.fastq.gz -> /shared/data/reads.pe1.fastq.gz
│   └── reads.pe2.fastq.gz -> /shared/data/reads.pe2.fastq.gz
├── tmp
│   ├── reads.pe1_fastqc.html
│   ├── reads.pe1_fastqc.zip
│   ├── reads.pe2_fastqc.html
│   └── reads.pe2_fastqc.zip

Now lets inspect those FastQC report generated!

Task

First, copy the output html files to the directory ~/www/tmp directory.

cp tmp/*_fastqc.html ~/www/tmp/

Then, open the browser and go to your personal module page (e.g., if your QMUL username is bob, the URL will be https://bob.genomicscourse.com) and click on the ~/www/tmp link.

After you should be presented with a screen that allows you to select the following HTML files to visualise.

Click the link to corresponding report files. You display should be similar to the image below.

Task

Question: What does the FastQC report tell you? Take 10 minutes to look through the following FASTQC documentation here to understand the purpose of each plot.

If you are still confused about Phred Scores, check out this page here

Question

QuestionAnswer

Which FastQC plots shows the relationship between base quality and position in the sequence? What else does this plot tell you about nucleotide composition towards the end of the sequences?

The Per Base Sequence Quality Plot

For each position a Box-Whisker type plot is drawn. The elements of the plot are as follows:

The central red line is the median value The yellow box represents the inter-quartile range (25-75%) The upper and lower whiskers represent the 10% and 90% points The blue line represents the mean quality The y-axis on the graph shows the quality scores.

Question

QuestionAnswer

How does the quality change across the read? Is it uniform?

Typically the average nucleotide quality declines towards the end of the read, meaning that the sequencing quality is not uniform across the entire read. This reduction in quality towards the 3′ end is common in sequencing data and can be caused by factors such as signal degradation during the sequencing process.

Question

QuestionAnswer

Comparing the per-base sequencing quality reports for reads.pe1.fastq.gz and reads.pe2.fastq.gz, which set has, on average, higher quality?

  • reads.pe1.fastq.gz

Question

QuestionAnswer

How could you handle low quality reads? Discuss this question with a partner before looking at the answer.

  • Discard entire reads that do not meet a specified quality threshold.
  • Trim low-quality regions from individual reads while retaining the higher-quality portions.

In the following sections, we will perform the following cleaning steps:

  • Trimming the ends of sequence reads using cutadapt.
  • K-mer filtering using the bioinformatics tool kmc3.
  • Removing sequences that are of low quality or too short using trimmomatic.

Other similar tools include fastx_toolkit, BBTools, and Trimmomatic however, we will not use them in this practical!

docs.title: Read trimming
docs.text:
To clean the FASTQ sequences, we will use a software tool called Trimmomatic. As stated on the official website: Trimmomatic is a flexible read trimming tool for Illumina NGS data. It performs a variety of useful trimming tasks for Illumina paired-end and single ended data.

To identify relevant quality cutoffs, it is necessary to be familiar with base quality scores and examine the per-base quality score in your FastQC report.

We will run Trimmomatic with several options: - LEADING: removes low quality bases from the beginning of the read - TRAILING: removes low quality bases from the end of the read - SLIDINGWINDOW: performs a sliding window trimming approach - MINLEN: removes reads that fall below the specified minimum length

Task

Take 5 minutes to review the trimmomatic documentation here to make sure you understand completely how the tool works. This is best practice for bioinformaticians when using a new tool for the first time and a good habit!

Task

The command to run Trimmomatic on the paired-end reads files is reported below. Trimmomatic processes both paired-end files simultaneously and produces four output files: two for paired reads that survived trimming and two for unpaired reads where only one of the pair survived.

cd ~/2026-09-22-read_cleaning

trimmomatic PE \
  input/reads.pe1.fastq.gz \
  input/reads.pe2.fastq.gz \
  tmp/reads.pe1.trimmed.fq \
  tmp/reads.pe1.unpaired.fq \
  tmp/reads.pe2.trimmed.fq \
  tmp/reads.pe2.unpaired.fq \
  LEADING:3 TRAILING:3 SLIDINGWINDOW:4:15 MINLEN:36

Note: You can adjust the quality parameters (LEADING, TRAILING, and SLIDINGWINDOW) based on your FastQC results.

Info

Note: If you trim too much of your sequence (i.e., too large values for LEADING, TRAILING, or too stringent SLIDINGWINDOW parameters), you increase the likelihood of eliminating important information. For this example, we suggest keeping quality thresholds around 3-5 for LEADING and TRAILING, and using a sliding window of 4:15 (window size:quality threshold).

Question

QuestionAnswer

When using Trimmomatic, does the order of trimming commands matter?

Yes. Trimmomatic executes trimming steps sequentially from left to right in the exact order specified on the command line. The output of each step becomes the input for the next.

Because commands run as a pipeline, the sequence directly impacts your output. For example it is best practice to:

  • Run Quality Trimming in a logical sequence. Steps like LEADING or TRAILING remove low-quality bases from the read edges before SLIDINGWINDOW evaluates broader region quality.

  • The SLIDINGWINDOW will scan the read 5' to 3' and cut the left most position in the window where the average quality drops below the threshold, subsequently removing the rest of the read.

  • The Minimum length filter (MINLEN) is typically the final step. If placed earlier, reads are checked before subsequent quality trimming shortens them, allowing reads that end up below your minimum length threshold to slip into your final file.

docs.title: 6. K-mer filtering, removal of short sequences
docs.text:
Let's suppose that you have sequenced your sample at 45x genome coverage. This means that every nucleotide of the genome was sequenced 45 times on average. So, for a genome of 100,000,000 nucleotides, you expect to have about 4,500,000,000 nucleotides of raw sequence. But that coverage will not be homogeneous. Instead, the real coverage distribution will be influenced by factors including DNA quality, library preparation type, how was DNA packaged within the chromosomes (e.g., hetero vs. euchromatin) and local GC content. But you might expect most of the genome to be covered between 20 and 70x.

In practice, this distribution can be very strange. One way of rapidly examining the coverage distribution before you have a reference genome is to chop your raw sequence reads into short "k-mers" of k nucleotides long, and estimate the frequency of occurrence of all k-mers. An example plot of k-mer frequencies from a haploid sample sequenced at ~45x coverage is shown below:

In the above plot, the y axis represents the proportion of k-mers in the dataset that are observed x times (called Coverage). As, expected, we observe a peak in the region close to 45, which corresponds to the targeted coverage.

However, we also see that a large fraction of sequences have a very low coverage (they are found only 10 times or less).

These rare k-mers are likely to be errors that appeared during library preparation or sequencing, or could be rare somatic mutations. Analogously (although not shown in the above plot) other k-mers may exist at very large coverage (up to 10,000). These could be viruses or other pathogens, or highly repetitive parts of the genome, such as transposable elements or simple repeats.

Info

Note: Extremely rare and extremely frequent sequences can both confuse assembly algorithms. Eliminating them can reduce subsequent memory, disk space and CPU requirements considerably, making overall computing more efficient and friendly.

Below, we use kmc3 to "mask" extremely rare k-mers (i.e., convert each base in the sequences corresponding to rare k-mers into N). In this way, we will ignore these bases (those called N) because they are not really present in the species. Multiple alternative approaches for k-mer filtering exist (e.g., using khmer).

Here, we use kmc3 to estimate the coverage of k-mers with a size of 21 nucleotides. When the masked k-mers are located at the end of the reads, we trim them in a subsequent step using cutadapt. If the masked k-mers are in the middle of the reads, we leave them just masked. Trimming reads (either masked k-mers or low quality ends in the previous step) can cause some reads to become too short to be informative. We remove such reads in the same step using cutadapt. Finally, discarding reads (because they are too short) can cause the corresponding read of the pair to become "unpaired". While it is possible to capture and use unpaired reads, we skip that here for simplicity. Understanding the exact commands – which are a bit convoluted – is unnecessary. However, it is important to understand the concept of k-mer filtering and the reasoning behind each step.

Task

Work through the following set of commands and before you run each one, try to understand what each step is doing!

To mask rare k-mers we will first build a k-mer database that includes counts for each k-mer. For this, we first make a list of files to input to KMC.

ls tmp/reads.pe1.trimmed.fq tmp/reads.pe2.trimmed.fq > tmp/file_list_for_kmc

Build a k-mer database using k-mer size of 21 nucleotides (-k). This will produce two files in your tmp/ directory: ./tmp/21-mers.kmc_pre and ./tmp/21-mers.kmc_suf. The last argument (tmp) tells kmc where to put intermediate files during computation; these are automatically deleted afterwards. The -m option tells KMC to use only 4 GB of RAM.

kmc -m4 -k21 @tmp/file_list_for_kmc tmp/21-mers tmp

Question

QuestionAnswer

As you were building the Kmer database a response was returned to the terminal, how did you interpret the output?

***************************************
Stage 1: 100%
Stage 2: 100%
1st stage: 6.42227s
2nd stage: 11.3654s
Total    : 17.7877s
Tmp size : 99MB

Stats:
No. of k-mers below min. threshold :      3595345
No. of k-mers above max. threshold :            0
No. of unique k-mers               :      7172390
No. of unique counted k-mers       :      3577045
Total no. of k-mers                :     80217049
Total no. of reads                 :       674112
Total no. of super-k-mers          :     12191773

This output summarise the metrics, temporary resource usage, and k-mer count statistics produced by KMC (K-mer Counter) after processing the set of reads provided.

Performance Metrics

  • Stage 1 & Stage 2 (100%): KMC completed both of its operational phases. Stage 1 partitions sequencing reads into disk bins via super-k-mers, and Stage 2 counts and sorts k-mers within each bin.

  • 1st stage / 2nd stage / Total: Stage 1 took ~6.42s, Stage 2 took ~11.37s, for a total run time of 17.79 seconds.

  • Tmp size (99MB): Peak disk space used for temporary bin files during processing.

Dataset & K-mer Statistics

  • Total no. of reads (674,112): Total number of sequencing reads read from the input files.
  • Total no. of k-mers (80,217,049): Cumulative count of all k-mers observed across all reads (includes all duplicates and repetitions).
  • Total no. of super-k-mers (12,191,773): Overlapping sequences of k-mers sharing identical signatures, generated during Stage 1 for efficient memory and disk management.
  • No. of unique k-mers (7,172,390): Total number of distinct k-mer sequences observed in the dataset before applying filters.
  • No. of k-mers below min. threshold (3,595,345): Distinct k-mers filtered out because their occurrence count fell below the minimum cutoff (-ci, usually set to 2 to eliminate sequencing errors).
  • No. of k-mers above max. threshold (0): Distinct k-mers filtered out for exceeding the maximum cutoff (-cx).
  • No. of unique counted k-mers (3,577,045): Distinct k-mers that passed all threshold filters and were written to the output database (7,172,390 - 3,595,345 = 3,577,045).

Task

Now the k-mer database is built it is time to continue!

Mask k-mers (-hm) observed less than two times (-ci) in the database (tmp/21-mers). The -t option tells KMC to run in single-threaded mode: this is required to preserve the order of the reads in the file. filter is a sub-command of kmc_tools that has options to mask, trim, or discard reads contain extremely rare k-mers.

Note: kmc_tools command may take a few seconds to complete and does not provide any visual feedback during the process.

kmc_tools -t1 filter -hm tmp/21-mers tmp/reads.pe1.trimmed.fq -ci2 tmp/reads.pe1.trimmed.norare.fq

kmc_tools -t1 filter -hm tmp/21-mers tmp/reads.pe2.trimmed.fq -ci2 tmp/reads.pe2.trimmed.norare.fq

Check if unpaired reads are present in the files

cutadapt -o /dev/null -p /dev/null tmp/reads.pe1.trimmed.norare.fq tmp/reads.pe2.trimmed.norare.fq

Trim 'N's from the ends of the reads, then discard reads shorter than 21 bp, and save remaining reads to the paths specified by -o and -p options. The -p option ensures that only paired reads are saved (an error is raised if unpaired reads are found).

cutadapt --trim-n --minimum-length 21 -o tmp/reads.pe1.clean.fq -p tmp/reads.pe2.clean.fq tmp/reads.pe1.trimmed.norare.fq tmp/reads.pe2.trimmed.norare.fq

Finally, we can copy over the cleaned reads to results directory for further analysis

cp tmp/reads.pe1.clean.fq tmp/reads.pe2.clean.fq results

Info

Note. If you are interested in understanding how KMC3 works at a deeper level, take a look the corresponding publication here, especially the supplementary information here

docs.title: 1. A brief assembly example
docs.text:
Many different pieces of software exist for genome assembly but as mentioned in the earlier lectures we will be using SPAdes.

Again for this practical you will be using the remote AWS computers created for you so please ssh back into these!

Task

Following the same procedure from the first read cleaning practical Part 1: Read cleaning, create a new main directory for today's practical (e.g., 2026-09-23-assembly), the input, tmp, and results subdirectories, and the file WHATIDID.txt to log your commands.

To help get you started 

mkdir 2026-09-23-assembly

Your directory hierarchy should look like the following

Terminal

2026-09-23-assembly
├── input
├── tmp
├── results
└── WHATIDID.txt

Next lets link the cleaned reads from yesterdays practical into our input subdirectory. We will be using these clean reads to create our assembly today!

Task

Use the following commands to achieve this! 

cd ~/2026-09-23-assembly
cd input
ln -s ~/2026-09-22-read_cleaning/results/reads.pe*.clean.fq .
cd ..

Question

QuestionAnswer

Did you note the use of * in the above command? What does this symbol do?

The symbol * is called a wildcard. In the shell, it matches any sequence of characters in filenames, so reads.pe*.clean.fq means “all files whose names start with reads.pe, then have any text in between, and end with .clean.fq. For example, it would match reads.pe1.clean.fq and reads.pe2.clean.fq, but not a file with a different name pattern. This is useful for working with many files at once without typing each name individually.

Task

To assemble our cleaned reads with SPAdes, run the following line: (This will take about 10 minutes)

spades.py -o tmp -1 input/reads.pe1.clean.fq -2 input/reads.pe2.clean.fq

Like any other assembler, SPAdes creates many files, including a scaffolds.fasta file that is likely to be used for follow-up analyses.

Copy this file to your results directory:

cp tmp/scaffolds.fasta results/

Take a look at the contents of this file (e.g., to see the first 10 lines, use head results/scaffolds.fasta, or tail results/scaffolds.fasta to see the last 10 lines).

Question

QuestionAnswer

Does it contain a lot of NNNN sequences? What do you think might be the reason for that? (Do not worry if your assembly does not contain any NNNN sequence.

N bases represent unknown nucleotide positions. In a SPAdes assembly, they are commonly introduced when contigs are joined into scaffolds across gaps where the reads do not provide enough information to determine the exact sequence, often because of repeats or insufficient read coverage. The number of N bases therefore reflects unresolved regions rather than actual nucleotides. An assembly with few or no N bases is also possible, particularly when it contains mostly contigs rather than scaffolds.

Task

While waiting for Spades to run please see if you can find the additional UNIX: command line learning material, uploaded to QMPlus.

To get an idea of some challenges associated with de novo genome assembly and the approaches used to overcome them, please review the following papers:

  • Towards complete and error-free genome assemblies of all vertebrate species. (Rhie et al 2021)
  • Long walk to genomics: History and current approaches to genome sequencing and assembly. (Giani et al 2020).
  • A hybrid approach for de novo human genome sequence assembly and phasing. Mostovoy et al (2016).
  • Genetic variation and the de novo assembly of human genomes. Chaisson et al 2015 NRG

docs.title: 2. Quality assessment
docs.text:
How do we know if our genome is good?

"... the performance of different de novo genome assembly algorithms can vary greatly on the same dataset, although it has been repeatedly demonstrated that no single assembler is optimal in every possible quality metric [6, 7, 8]. The most widely used metrics for evaluating an assembly include 1) contiguity statistics such as scaffold and contig N50 size, 2) accuracy statistics such as the number of structural errors found when compared with an available reference genome (GAGE (Genome Assembly Gold Standard Evaluation) evaluation tool [8]), 3) presence of core eukaryotic genes (CEGMA (Core Eukaryotic Genes Mapping Approach) [9]) or, if available, transcript mapping rates, and 4) the concordance of the sequence with remapped paired-end and mate-pair reads (REAPR (Recognizing Errors in Assemblies using Paired Reads) [10], assembly validation [11], or assembly likelihood [12])." - Wences & Schatz (2015)

docs.title: 2.1 Simple metrics
docs.text:
An assembly software will generally provide some statistics about what it did. But, note that the output formats may differ between assemblers. Quast, the Quality Assessment Tool for Genome Assemblies is a tool designed to generate a standardized report.

Task

Run Quast on the scaffolds.fasta file without special options to get the basic statistics:

cd ~/2026-09-23-assembly/results
quast.py scaffolds.fasta

Have a look at the report (pdf or html) generated by Quast (copy the Quast's output directory to ~/www/tmp and access through your browser).

cp quast_results/latest/report.html ~/www/tmp

Question

QuestionAnswer

Looking at the assembly metrics in the QUAST report? For which metrics is a higher or smaller value better?

A Higher Value is Better

  • N50, N90: Higher values indicate greater assembly contiguity, meaning larger contiguous sequences make up the core of the assembly.

  • Largest contig: A longer maximum contig length reflects fewer assembly breakpoints across major genomic regions.

A Smaller Value is Better

  • L50 and L90: Lower values mean fewer contigs are required to cover 50 percent or 90 percent of the assembly total length.

  • Number of Ns / Ns per 100 kbp: Fewer ambiguous bases indicate higher sequence completeness and accuracy within scaffolds.

Context-Dependent

  • Number of contigs: Fewer total contigs generally indicate a less fragmented, more contiguous assembly. However, this metric must be evaluated alongside total assembly length as an artificially low contig count can simply indicate an incomplete assembly that missed large genomic regions.

  • Total length: Total length should closely approximate the expected genome size of the target organism. An assembly significantly smaller than expected suggests missing sequence or collapsed repeats, whereas a substantially larger assembly may indicate sample contamination or underlying high error rate..

  • GC percentage: Neither higher nor lower is inherently better, instead this value should closely match the known baseline GC content of the target organism.

Task

Using your web-browser of choice see if you can find the expected GC content of the complete Fire Ant genome? Does the GC content of the assembly match what is expected?

docs.title: 2.2 Biologically meaningful measures
docs.text:
Unfortunately, with many of the simple metrics, it is difficult to determine whether the assembler did things correctly, or just haphazardly stuck lots of reads together.

We often have other prior information about what to expect in this genome. For example:

  1. if we have a reference assembly from a not-too-distant relative, we can expect that large genome parts will be organised in the same order, i.e., synteny.
  2. If we independently created a transcriptome assembly, we can expect that the exons making each transcript will be mapped sequentially onto the genome (see TGNet for an implementation).
  3. We can expect different patterns of gene content and structure between eukaryotes and prokaryotes.
  4. Pushing this idea further, we can expect a genome to contain a single copy of each of the "house-keeping" genes found in related species. This is applied in BUSCO (Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs). Note that:
    • BUSCO is a refined, modernized implementation of CEGMA (Core Eukaryotic Genes Mapping Approach). CEGMA examines a eukaryotic genome assembly for the presence and completeness of 248 "core eukaryotic genes".
    • Quast also includes a "quick and dirty" method of finding genes.
  5. We can expect that the different scaffolds in the genome have a unimodal distribution in sequence read coverage. Similarly, we can expect that the percentage of GC content will be unimodally distributed among scaffolds. Using this idea, the Blobology approach determined that evidence of foreign sequences in Tardigrades is largely due to extensive contamination rather than extensive horizontal gene transfer Koutsovoulos et al 2016.

It is important to understand the concepts underlying these different approaches.
